card.title: How attention hides later tokens
card.question: how does attention hide later tokens?

brief.prose: Each token is only allowed to look at itself and the tokens before it. Scores for later positions are blanked out so they get zero weight.

standard.prose: The constructor checks whether PyTorch has a fused attention function and stores the answer in `self.flash`. If it does, line 64 passes `is_causal=True`, so the fused kernel applies the left-to-right mask itself. Otherwise the constructor builds a lower-triangular matrix of ones with `torch.tril` and stores it as the buffer `bias`. In the manual path, line 67 computes the query-key scores, a (T, T) grid per head. Line 68 then uses `masked_fill` to set every score to minus infinity wherever the triangular matrix is 0, which is every position after the current one. Softmax on line 69 turns minus infinity into a weight of exactly zero, so later tokens contribute nothing. The weights then pass through dropout and multiply `v` on lines 70-71, so each output mixes only the current and earlier tokens. The slice `[:,:,:T,:T]` trims the stored mask to the actual sequence length.

detailed.prose: The constructor checks for the fused function and stores the result in `self.flash`. If it exists, line 64 passes `is_causal=True`, and the mask is applied inside the kernel, so no mask buffer is needed. Otherwise the constructor builds a lower-triangular matrix of ones as the buffer `bias`. Row i of that matrix has ones in columns 0 to i, so query i may see keys 0 to i. Line 67 computes the scaled scores with shape (B, nh, T, T). Line 68 fills the zero entries of the mask with minus infinity, using the mask sliced to T. Softmax over the last dimension then gives those entries a weight of exactly zero, and the remaining weights sum to 1. Dropout and the multiply by `v` follow. The comment on line 48 says attention applies only to the left, which matches the code. The buffer is sized by block_size, which is why the slice is needed for shorter inputs.

steps: The scores form a 3x3 grid s[i][j].
Softmax of row 1 gives two positive weights that sum to 1, then 0.
The output at position 0 is exactly v0, since it can only see itself.

An argument without an equals sign is treated as a config file, which is read, printed and exec'd, so its assignments overwrite globals. An argument with an equals sign must start with two dashes, and the text before the equals sign, minus the dashes, becomes the key. An assert requires the new value's type to match the existing variable's type, so a bad type stops the run. card.title: Why the output begins with your start text
card.question: why does the output start with my --start text?

brief.prose: Your start text is turned into tokens and handed to the model as the beginning of the sequence. The model only appends to it, and the whole sequence is printed, so your text comes back first.

standard.prose: If start begins with FILE:, the text is read from that file instead. Then `encode` turns the start string into a list of token ids, `start_ids`. Those ids become a tensor `x` with a leading batch dimension. For each sample, `model.generate` is called with `x` as the context to continue. The result `y` is the prompt ids followed by the new ids, so the prompt is part of it. `decode(y[0].tolist())` turns the whole row back into text and prints it, which is why your start text appears first. Nothing in these lines strips the prompt off. I would need model.py's `generate` to confirm it appends new tokens to `x` and returns the full sequence.

detailed.prose: If start begins with FILE:, the text is read from that file instead. Then `encode` turns the start string into token ids. Which encoder is used depends on whether a meta.pkl was found. With meta.pkl, encoding is per character. Otherwise it uses GPT-2 BPE. The ids become a tensor `x` of shape (1, T). `model.generate` receives `x` as context. Its return `y` is indexed with `y[0]`, so the prompt ids are in the row you decode. The decode call reverses the same encoding and prints everything. So the prompt is echoed because it is never removed. I would need model.py's `generate` to confirm that it appends to `x`.

card.title: How the learning rate warms up, then decays
card.question: how does the learning rate change over training?

brief.prose: The learning rate ramps up from near zero, then glides down smoothly to a small floor value. After that it stays flat at the floor.

standard.prose: get_lr takes the step number it and returns the learning rate for that step. For the first warmup_iters steps, it returns learning_rate scaled by (it + 1) / (warmup_iters + 1), a straight-line ramp up. Once it passes lr_decay_iters, it returns the constant min_lr. In between, decay_ratio measures how far you are through the decay span, from 0 to 1. The assert on the next line guards that range. coeff is half of 1 plus cosine of pi times decay_ratio, so it slides from 1 to 0 along a cosine curve. The result is min_lr plus coeff times the gap between learning_rate and min_lr, so the rate falls smoothly from learning_rate to min_lr. The actual values of warmup_iters, learning_rate, lr_decay_iters and min_lr are set in config files such as the shakespeare_char config, not in these lines.

card.title: What the sampling settings in sample.py control
card.question: what do these settings do?

brief.prose: These are the defaults for generating text from a trained model: where the model comes from, how much to write, and how adventurous the word choice is. Any of them can be overridden from the command line or a config file.

The `out_dir` line is the checkpoint folder and is ignored unless `init_from` is 'resume', so a wrong folder only matters in resume mode. The `start` line is the prompt text, and a value of the form FILE:prompt.txt reads the prompt from a file. The `num_samples` and `max_new_tokens` lines set how many samples are drawn and how many tokens each one gets, so larger values mean longer runs. The `temperature` line scales randomness: below 1.0 is less random and above 1.0 is more random. The `top_k` line keeps only the most likely tokens and clamps the rest to zero probability, so a very small value would make output repetitive. The `seed` line fixes the random seed for repeatable output. The `device` line names the hardware, and 'cuda' on a machine without a GPU would likely fail. The `dtype` line chooses bfloat16 if CUDA reports support and float16 otherwise. The `compile` line turns PyTorch 2.0 compilation on or off. The final line runs configurator.py, which overrides any of these names from the command line or a config file. How it applies overrides is in configurator.py, which I cannot see here.
